18vss6:2015: Implementing an Agentic Scheduler on Strands and AgentCore for automatic orchestration of inference GPU capacity across multiple Regions by awschina on 25 Feb 2026 in Management Tools Permalink Share Background and Requirements When deploying large-model inference and elastic scaling within a single region, e.g., Singapore, we often encounter unsupported GPU types such as G6/G6e or G5. Or GPU instances fail to start due to insufficient capacity (e.g., InsufficientInstanceCapacity), making scaling results unpredictable, delivery cycles passively longer, and affecting online service stability and SLA. Traditional approaches that rely on engineers manually switching availability zones and repeatedly trying across regions are inefficient, hard to scale, and lack traceable decision basis and standardized processes. To solve this, we implemented a cross-region GPU scheduling solution based on Strands Agents: the system accepts natural-language capacity requests (instance type, target count, preferred region, network constraints, etc.), automatically generates a candidate Region/AZ list with scoring/ranking, and attempts launches step by step according to plan; when capacity shortage, quota shortage, or network/permission errors occur, the Agent dynamically adjusts its strategy based on error classification (switching AZ/Region, launching in batches, etc.) until the target capacity is met or retry budget is exhausted. The scheduling Agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, and writes the input, plan version, attempt records, and final result of each schedule into AgentCore Memory, supporting replay and review by requestId, continuously improving strategy hit rate and operability. On the engineering practice front, this project used Kiro IDE's Specs-driven approach throughout, from Requirements → Design → Implementation, turning requirements, architecture decisions, and task breakdowns into versioned assets, ensuring that the complex Agentic system remains traceable, auditable, testable, and has a reproducible delivery path during rapid iteration. Overall Architecture Overall Feature Highlights 1. LLM-based Agent for cross-region GPU demand orchestration Compared with traditional rule-based GPU scheduling and launch control, an LLM-based Agent is better suited to handling highly uncertain, strongly context-dependent problems such as cloud capacity fluctuation. Rule systems typically rely on hardcoded if/else and static priorities: once they encounter uncovered error combinations (capacity shortage plus quota constraints, AZ offering differences, network routing restrictions, permission gaps, etc.), they either fail and exit or require manual intervention to add rules, with high iteration cost and a tendency to form a "rule quagmire". An LLM Agent, in contrast, treats a launch process as a closed loop of "plan → execute → observe → re-plan": it understands business intent and constraints in natural language or structured input (e.g., prefer Singapore, must land in the specified subnet, allow cross-region fallback, retry budget limits), dynamically adjusts strategy at execution time based on real-time error codes and context (switching AZ/Region, splitting batches, changing attempt order, giving quota/permission remediation suggestions), and generates explainable decision rationale and a final report. LLM-based Agents are naturally more extensible than rule engines: adding or adjusting Regions often does not require large-scale code changes or piling up if/else; it is enough to include the new Region in the candidate pool and supplement a small amount of "environment facts" (e.g., available instance types, quotas, and network constraints) for the Agent to complete judgment and orchestration at runtime. This turns "supporting more Regions" from a one-time engineering transformation into sustainable configuration-driven expansion and strategy iteration. This capability is especially suitable for GPU scenarios with significant capacity fluctuation and regional differences, significantly reducing the cost of launching new Regions and improving the adaptation speed of global scheduling. 2. Additional value from deploying on AgentCore Runtime and Memory Deploying the Agent-based cross-region GPU provisioning system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and AgentCore Memory upgrades "scheduling logic" from one-off scripts to an operable, extensible production-grade service. First, AgentCore Runtime provides a managed runtime environment and session-level isolation, enabling the scheduling Agent to handle multi-step orchestration with a stable execution context (candidate Region generation, offerings/quota pre-checks, batch launches, failure diagnosis, and re-planning), and supports elastic scaling by request concurrency, reducing the operational burden of building your own runtime framework, container governance, and permission orchestration. Second, AgentCore Memory is responsible for saving conversation memory, recording the interaction process between user and Agent. store_conversation stores user messages, Agent replies, approval requests/responses, etc. into the AgentCore Memory service on each request/response. In addition, there is LTM (long-term memory) functionality: retrieve_ltm_context extracts historical scheduling experience via semantic search and injects it into the system prompt, allowing the Agent to "remember" previous capacity scheduling experience (e.g., which region is often out of stock). 3.
